paras: The lynching of an unidentified Black man near Alto, Texas, was reported on July 31, 1903, after a crowd took the man from a constable who had arrested him for allegedly cursing women and firing into their house. A Dallas News special carried by the Associated Press said he was lynched in the river bottom by a mob, while a report from Tyler said searching parties had not found his body. The item ran in at least seventeen white newspapers, several of which headlined the accusation as the reason for the killing.

Alto was described as a small town fifty miles south of Tyler on the Cotton Belt railroad. According to the Dallas News special, the man had insulted "some ladies" by cursing them and firing into their house. The Tyler report gave a fuller version of the accusation, saying he was drunk and shot into a house occupied by a number of women and children.

A constable arrested the man, and soon afterward a crowd of thirty took him away from the officer and started toward a bottom. The Dallas special said he was lynched "in the river bottom by a mob," and one digest said he was taken a few miles from town before he was lynched. No report gave his name, the method of killing, or the names of anyone in the crowd.

The Tyler dispatch said searching parties had failed to find the body by one o'clock in the morning, and it described the lynching only as a report that had reached the town. No later confirmation of the death, inquest, or arrest appears in the coverage.

Southern dailies printed the Dallas News special between August 1 and August 5 under headlines such as "Lynched for Insulting Ladies" in Wilmington, "Negro Lynched in Texas" in Atlanta, and "Negro Reported Lynched" in Birmingham. In the Richmond Times Dispatch the key word dropped out, leaving the man "in the river bottom by a mob" under the headline "Negro Was Lynched for Insulting Ladies."

Western papers ran a shorter version datelined Alto that called the victim "an unknown negro" and said he was lynched "here today," with the Phoenix Arizona Republican heading it "Lynched for Cursing" and the Topeka State Journal "Didn't Know His Name." Weekly news digests in South Dakota, Minnesota, and Nebraska repeated the same sentence through mid-August, sometimes amid items on other lynchings. Only the Shiner Gazette's Tyler item, headed "Negro Reported Lynched," attributed each detail to "the report" and noted that the body had not been found. No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.
The wire items stated the lynching as fact, while the Tyler report, the only account with details of the arrest and seizure, treated the death as unconfirmed.

reader.title: Lynching of an unidentified Black man near Alto, Texas
bases: Every report says a mob lynched the man, and the one detailed account says a crowd of thirty took him from a constable after his arrest (A6, A11).

A crowd of thirty took an arrested man from a constable over an accusation of cursing women and firing into their house, and the wire reported him lynched (A6, A11); but the Tyler report called the lynching a report only and said searching parties had not found the body (A11).

The Dallas News special (A6) and a separately worded Tyler report (A11) agree that a crowd seized a Black man at or near Alto over the shooting into a house, though only the Dallas version states the lynching as fact.

accounts.label: Tyler report
accounts.gist: A report reached Tyler that a drunk Black man who shot into a house of women and children was arrested by a constable, taken from him by a crowd of thirty toward a bottom, and lynched; searching parties had not found the body.

framing.detail: Southern dailies ran the Dallas News special under headlines such as 'Lynched for Insulting Ladies' and 'Negro Lynched in Texas', giving the accusation as the reason without comment.
The Shiner Gazette's Tyler item was headed 'Negro Reported Lynched' and attributed every detail to 'the report'.
Western and Midwestern papers and weekly digests carried a one-sentence version, headed 'Lynched for Cursing' in Phoenix and 'Didn't Know His Name' in Topeka.

versions.value: Lynching reported; body not found by searching parties

conflicts.note: The Tyler report is the only one with details of the arrest and seizure and treats the death as unconfirmed; the wire items state it flatly. No later confirmation was found.
All texts describe the same wire wording; the Tyler report's 'yesterday evening' (from an Aug. 1 dateline) and 'Friday' in the weekly digests both point to July 31.
